newsitem.title: CHINA: China's political rifts exposed before Deng rites.
newsitem.headline: China's political rifts exposed before Deng rites.

text.p: China prepared on Sunday for its funeral of the decade, striving to present an image of unity following the death of Deng Xiaoping but already exposing deep-lying political fault lines.

Mindful of the tumult that erupted after the passing of previous Chinese strongmen, authorities threw a tight security net over the sites where final tributes are to be paid to Deng, who died on Wednesday at 92.

Deng's handpicked successor, Soviet-trained technocrat Jiang Zemin, has been quick to reassure his 1.2 billion countrymen that he will pursue, and even accelerate, the open-door policies that have transformed China.

But while unity, stability and continuity are the current watchwords of the official media, old enmities have not been buried, raising the spectre of power plays in the aftermath of a stressful transition.

A Chinese source said on Sunday that Jiang had refused a request from his predecessor, disgraced Communist Party chief Zhao Ziyang who is under virtual house arrest, to join the 10,000 people attending Deng's memorial ceremony in Beijing's Great Hall of the People on Tuesday.
Jiang gave no reason for barring Zhao from the rites honouring the man who appointed both men in turn to China's top job, the source told Reuters.

Deng handpicked Zhao as his successor in 1987 only to sack him two years later for sympathising with student demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square before they were crushed by the military, on Deng's orders, in June 1989.

Jiang, who replaced him as party chief and now also holds the posts of state president and head of the military, rejected Zhao's request even though Deng's family and some party veterans had agreed to allow him to attend, the source said.

Surveillance of Zhao was expected to tighten in the run-up to a crucial party congress later this year, the source said, as Jiang tries to cement his hold on power after the death of his powerful protector.
Diplomats say China's current leadership remains nervous of the influence of Zhao, whose relatively liberal policies made him popular while in office.
In addition, China's top conservative ideologue, Deng Liqun, has been left off the high-profile funeral committee for Deng at the request of the dead man's family, Chinese sources said.
"Deng Xiaoping's children did not want Deng Liqun on the funeral committee," said one source with close ties to the Communist Party.

The family was opposed to Deng Liqun sitting on the funeral committee because of his open criticism of Deng Xiaoping after the patriarch's 1992 tour of southern China that kick-started a faltering economy, the source said.
Deng Liqun, who is not related to the late paramount leader, was China's propaganda chief for several years under Deng and had been personally loyal to him for years.
Even as Deng lay on his deathbed, signs emerged of opposition to Jiang, who as head of party, government and military is now unarguably the most powerful man in China.
The February issue of China's most conservative magazine, Zhongliu, or Mainstay, attacked a book seen as pro-Jiang.
"It was the first cannon fired by leftists at Jiang Zemin," a political analyst said of the magazine, mouthpiece of Communist Party hardliners.
In contrast to the elaborate farewell traditionally accorded to Chinese heroes and strongmen, the last rites for Deng will be relatively simple, to the disappointment of some.
"I came all the way from Changchun (in northeast China) to see him," said farmer Hao Xingchang, who wept when he heard that Deng was to be cremated and that his body would not go on view.
"Under the policies before Deng Xiaoping we farmers were hungry. Only under Deng Xiaoping's policies could we eat our fill," he said.

Farmer Hao reflected the view of many Chinese who, whether or not they liked Deng, appreciated that his capitalist-style reforms had put money in their pockets after decades of politically correct poverty under his predecessor, Mao Zedong.
